What does this figure tell us about index variables?|date=August 2024}}]]
[[File:Social Vulnerability Index variables grouped into four themes.png|thumb|CDC/ATSDR Social Vulnerability Index variables grouped into four themes]]
In statistics and [[research design]], an '''index''' is a [[composite statistic]] – a measure of changes in a representative group of individual data points, or in other words, a compound measure that aggregates multiple [[Indicator (statistics)|indicator]]s.<ref name=HawkenMunck>{{cite journal|last1=Hawken|first1=Angela|last2=Munck|first2=Gerardo L.|title=Cross-National Indices with Gender-Differentiated Data: What Do They Measure? How Valid Are They?|journal=Social Indicators Research|date=24 April 2012|volume=111|issue=3|pages=801–838|doi=10.1007/s11205-012-0035-7|s2cid=144274479 }}</ref><ref name = "Babbie2012–159">{{cite book|author=Earl Babbie|title=The Practice of Social Research|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=k-aza3qSULoC&pg=PA159|date=1 January 2012|publisher=Cengage Learning|isbn=978-1-133-04979-1|page=159}}</ref> Indices – also known as '''indexes''' and '''composite indicators''' – summarize and rank specific observations.<ref name="Babbie2012–159" />

Much data in the field of social sciences and sustainability are represented in various indices such as [[Gender Gap Index]], [[Human Development Index]] or the [[Dow Jones Industrial Average]]. The ‘Report by the Commission on the Measurement of Economic Performance and Social Progress’, written by [[Joseph Stiglitz]], [[Amartya Sen]], and [[Jean-Paul Fitoussi]] in 2009 <ref name="Stiglitz">Stiglitz, J., Sen, A., & Fitoussi, J.-P. (2009). [Report by the Commission on the Measurement of Economic Performance and Social Progress.] </ref> suggests that these measures have experienced a dramatic growth in recent years due to three concurring factors: 

* improvements in the level of literacy (including statistical) 
* increased complexity of modern societies and economies, and 
* widespread availability of information technology. 

According to Earl Babbie, items in indices are usually weighted equally, unless there are some reasons against it (for example, if two items reflect essentially the same aspect of a variable, they could have a weight of 0.5 each).<ref name="Babbie2012-170">{{cite book|url = https://books.google.com/books?id=k-aza3qSULoC&pg=PA170|title = The Practice of Social Research|date = 1 January 2012|publisher = Cengage Learning|isbn = 978-1-133-04979-1|page = 162|author = Earl Babbie}}</ref>

According to the same author,<ref name="Babbie2012-185">{{cite book|author=Earl Babbie|title=The Practice of Social Research|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=k-aza3qSULoC&pg=PA185|date=1 January 2012|publisher=Cengage Learning|isbn=978-1-133-04979-1|page=185}}</ref> constructing the items involves four steps. First, items should be selected based on their [[content validity]], unidimensionality, the degree of [[Sensitivity and specificity|specificity]] in which a dimension is to be measured, and their amount of [[variance]]. Items should be empirically related to one another, which leads to the second step of examining their multivariate relationships. Third, index scores are designed, which involves determining score ranges and weights for the items. Finally, indices should be validated, which involves testing whether they can predict indicators related to the measured variable not used in their construction.<ref name="Babbie2012-185"/>

A handbook for the construction of composite indicators (CIs) was published jointly by the [[OECD]] and by the European Commission's [[Joint Research Centre]] in 2008.<ref name="OECD-JRC">OECD-JRC (2008). Handbook on constructing composite indicators: Methodology and user guide, OECD Statistics working paper JT00188147, STD/DOC(2005)3.</ref> The handbook – officially endorsed by the OECD high level statistical committee, describe ten recursive steps for developing an index:<ref>[https://composite-indicators.jrc.ec.europa.eu/?q=10-step-guide JRC web pages on composite indicators]</ref>

*Step 1: Theoretical framework
*Step 2: Data selection
*Step 3: Imputation of missing data
*Step 4: Multivariate analysis
*Step 5: Normalisation
*Step 6: Weighting
*Step 7: Aggregating indicators
*Step 8: Sensitivity analysis
*Step 9: Link to other measures
*Step 10: Visualisation

As suggested by the list, many modelling choices are needed to construct a composite indicator, which makes their use controversial.<ref name="OECD-JRC"/> The delicate issue of assigning and validating weights is discussed e.g. in.<ref>Becker W., Paruolo P., Saisana M., Saltelli A. (2017) Weights and Importance in Composite Indicators: Mind the Gap. In: Ghanem R., Higdon D., Owhadi H. (eds) Handbook of Uncertainty Quantification. Springer.</ref> A sociological reading of the nature of composite indicators is offered by [[Paul-Marie Boulanger]], who sees these measures at the intersection of three movements:<ref name="Boulanger_2014">Boulanger, P.-M. (2014). [http://publications.jrc.ec.europa.eu/repository/bitstream/JRC92162/lbna26921enn.pdf Elements for a comprehensive assessment of public indicators, Report EUR 26921 EN.]</ref> 

* the democratisation of expertise, the concept that more knowledge is needed to tackle societal and environmental issues that can be provided by the sole experts – this line of thought connects to the concept of extended peer community developed by [[post-normal science]]
* the impulse to the creation of a new public through a process of social discovery, which can be reconnected to the work of pragmatists such as [[John Dewey]]
* the [[semiotic]] of [[Charles Sanders Peirce]]; Thus a CI is not just a sign or a number, but suggests an action or a behaviour. 
 
A subsequent work by Boulanger <ref name="Boulanger:2018">Boulanger, P.-M. (2018). A systems-theoretical perspective on sustainable development and indicators. In S. Bell & S. Morse (Eds.), The Routledge handbook of sustainability indicators. London: Taylor & Francis.</ref> analyses composite indicators in light of the social system theories of [[Niklas Luhmann]] to investigate how different measurements of progress are or are not taken up.
